clinicalPearls: A localised keratoderma in which thick hyperkeratotic plaques or callosities form at sites of recurrent pressure and friction, chiefly the weight-bearing soles and the palms, rather than diffusely covering the palms and soles.
Lesions are frequently painful, particularly on the plantar surface, and can markedly impair walking, giving rise to the older term hereditary painful callosities.
Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant; nonepidermolytic focal forms are associated with variants in the keratin genes KRT16 and KRT6C.
Focal PPK overlaps with the pachyonychia congenita spectrum, which is also keratin-driven, so nail dystrophy, oral leukokeratosis and follicular keratoses should be sought.
Striate palmoplantar keratoderma, with linear streaks along the fingers and focal plantar plaques, is a related focal pattern caused by desmosomal gene variants (DSG1, DSP) or KRT1.
Histology of nonepidermolytic forms lacks the epidermolytic (vacuolar) change seen in epidermolytic keratoderma, which aids classification.
Management is largely mechanical and keratolytic, using offloading, emollients, keratolytics and careful debridement, with attention to fissuring and secondary infection.
Variants in the cation channel gene TRPV3 and other differentiation genes underlie some focal or mixed keratodermas, so precise genotyping guides counselling.
reference.pathophysiology: Focal palmoplantar keratoderma is a genetically heterogeneous disorder of terminal keratinocyte differentiation and mechanical resilience in acral epidermis. The commonest nonepidermolytic focal forms arise from dominant variants in the keratin genes KRT16 (which is also implicated in pachyonychia congenita) and KRT6C, which disrupt the keratin intermediate-filament cytoskeleton so that suprabasal keratinocytes cannot withstand mechanical stress, provoking compensatory hyperkeratosis at pressure sites. Striate variants result from haploinsufficiency or dominant-negative effects in desmosomal components (desmoglein-1, DSG1; desmoplakin, DSP) or in keratin 1 (KRT1), weakening cell-to-cell adhesion along lines of tension. Additional focal or mixed keratodermas are caused by variants in the transient receptor potential cation channel gene TRPV3 and other differentiation-related genes. The unifying mechanism is site-specific failure of epidermal barrier and cytoskeletal integrity under friction, distinguishing focal from diffuse (whole-surface) and punctate (discrete papular) patterns.
additionalDifferentials: Diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma (e.g., Vorner/Unna-Thost epidermolytic and nonepidermolytic diffuse forms)
Pachyonychia congenita, with focal plantar keratoderma and nail dystrophy
Acquired keratoderma (mechanical, inflammatory, drug-induced or paraneoplastic)
Palmoplantar psoriasis and tinea manuum or pedis
Pitted keratolysis and other localised plantar dermatoses
additionalInvestigations: Detailed personal and family history with a pedigree, usually showing autosomal dominant inheritance
Skin biopsy to distinguish epidermolytic from nonepidermolytic histology
Targeted keratin and keratoderma gene panel (KRT16, KRT6C, TRPV3, DSG1, DSP, KRT1)
Examination of nails, hair, teeth and oral mucosa for pachyonychia congenita features
Mycology of skin scrapings and culture to exclude dermatophyte infection
Podiatric assessment of gait and plantar pressure loading
Screening of relatives and genetic counselling
redFlags: Sudden or rapidly progressive keratoderma appearing in adulthood, raising the possibility of an acquired or paraneoplastic cause
Painful fissuring complicated by cellulitis or systemic infection
Associated oral leukokeratosis or laryngeal involvement threatening the airway within the spectrum overlap
Marked functional impairment of walking or hand use
reference.prognosis: A chronic and generally non-life-threatening condition; lesions persist and often cause pain and functional limitation, but consistent mechanical care and keratolytic treatment usually maintain reasonable function without shortening life.
pitfalls: Treating recalcitrant plantar plaques as simple corns or verrucae and missing an inherited keratoderma
Failing to look for the nail and mucosal signs of the pachyonychia congenita spectrum
Not distinguishing epidermolytic from nonepidermolytic forms, which affects genetic counselling
Overlooking an acquired or paraneoplastic keratoderma presenting focally in later life
Aggressive paring that causes painful erosions and secondary infection
management: Topical keratolytics such as salicylic acid and urea preparations with emollients to soften and reduce hyperkeratotic plaques
Regular mechanical paring of callosities, protective padding, cushioned footwear and orthotics to redistribute pressure and reduce pain
Topical retinoids, with oral retinoids such as acitretin reserved for severe, disabling disease and balanced against side effects
Podiatric assessment of gait and plantar pressure loading to guide offloading
Exclusion of dermatophyte superinfection by mycology, with antifungal treatment where present
Genetic counselling with a keratin and keratoderma gene panel given autosomal dominant inheritance, and evaluation for overlapping pachyonychia congenita features
Dermatology follow-up for chronic symptom control
